prize_parts.citation: For establishing how electrons tunnel over long distances through proteins, quantifying the dependence on distance, driving force and reorganization energy

statement.case_for: Gray and Winkler's ruthenium-modified protein experiments turned long-range biological electron transfer into a quantitative physical-chemical problem: rates measured over defined distances in a defined protein framework, with driving force and reorganization energy varied systematically, and with hopping mechanisms later identified for multistep chains. That framework is used to interpret respiratory and photosynthetic enzymes. The attribution is bounded and the two-person configuration is clean. The work is decades old and independently confirmed, so recognition is neither premature nor contested on priority. It builds on the 1992 Marcus prize rather than repeating it, because the new content is experimental demonstration of tunneling through the protein medium and the physical principles that follow.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the committee may regard this as the experimental continuation of Marcus theory, which was recognized in 1992. Credit for the tunneling-pathway picture also involves Beratan, Onuchic, Dutton and others, and a two-person prize would leave them out. I also have to flag that my own field sits close to this topic, so I should not let familiarity inflate its standing against candidates with much broader consequences. B006 received first place only from me in the openings, so it has the weakest opening support of any of my top choices, and I should not present that as consensus.

responses.point: Daniel Aili ranked targeted protein degradation first as a new event-driven modality that is already clinical-stage, with Crews, Deshaies and Handa as the core, while granting that timing is arguable because no approved PROTAC drug is established.
responses.response: I agree with Daniel that B045 is the most strongly supported candidacy in the opening round and that the mechanism, including the cereblon identification, is well confirmed. My reservation is the attribution and the clinical maturity. The PROTAC concept, the cereblon discovery, VHL ligand design and the first Sakamoto and Kim work are distinct achievements, and three names exclude Ciulli, Sakamoto, Kim, Gray and Ito. I would also want the expert reports to say whether clinical benefit has been shown beyond the early trials. I keep B045 as my first alternative, but I do not think its crowded credit is a minor point.

responses.point: Peter Somfai put Pd-catalyzed C-N cross-coupling first, arguing that Buchwald and Hartwig developed general catalyst systems independently, that the area is mature and overdue, and that a two-person prize is clean.
responses.response: Peter makes the attribution case that is hardest for me to counter, because the Buchwald and Hartwig pairing is cleaner than most on the shortlist and the maturity is not in doubt. My difficulty is the 2010 cross-coupling prize. The committee will need to be convinced that C-N coupling is a distinct achievement with ligand-design logic that the 2010 recognition did not cover, rather than an extension of Pd cross-coupling. If the expert reports support that distinction, B069 would deserve to rank above several candidates I put higher, and I would not oppose it. On the criterion I care about, mechanistic understanding, I would like to see how much of the case rests on mechanism and how much on utility in synthesis.

responses.point: Heiner Linke ranked dye-sensitized solar cells first, arguing that a sensitized mesoscopic TiO2 film separates absorption from charge transport, with O'Regan and Grätzel as the decisive pair and the mechanism quantified through injection and recombination kinetics.
responses.response: I share Heiner's preference for candidates built on a clear physical principle with measured kinetics, and the electron injection and recombination story in B018 is close in spirit to B006, since both are about how charge moves through a molecular-scale medium. I disagree on one point. The device achievement of B018 has been commercially modest, and the case rests on the conceptual opening of molecular photovoltaics, which the later perovskite work partly overtook. I would also ask whether Hagfeldt's contribution is more than incremental. I find B018 and B006 comparable on mechanism, and I would not argue that either has a decisive advantage on maturity.

responses.point: Emma Sparr ranked biomolecular condensates first as a unifying physical-chemical principle of liquid-liquid phase separation, while noting the credit is crowded around Pappu and Mittag.
responses.response: I agree with Emma that phase separation is a real physical principle and has reorganized how cells are described. My concern is that the debate on in vivo relevance, on the definition of a condensate and on liquid versus gel states is still active, which makes this the least settled of the leading candidacies in my view. The attribution among Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen, Pappu and Mittag is also unresolved. A Nobel should reward a result that survives that debate, and I would wait for the expert reports to say whether it has.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats B006 as a distinct achievement from the 1992 Marcus prize.
Whether the tunneling-pathway contributions of others make a two-person award for B006 unfair.
Whether C-N cross-coupling (B069) is sufficiently distinct from the 2010 cross-coupling prize.
Whether the clinical evidence for degraders (B045) is mature enough, and how to limit the credit to three names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. I note that my research field (biological energy conversion, electron and proton transfer) is close to B006 and B022, and that I am a Stockholm University colleague of Xiaodong Zou, though none of the shortlisted candidates is connected to either of us personally.
